workers with decreased work abilities are at risk for reduced productivity, and that job control is an important determinant for workers with decreased abilities to remain productive.
workers with decreased work capacity are less productive at work, and that this negative effect can partly be compensated by increased job control.
workers with decreased work capacity were more likely to experience productivity loss at work, and this was particularly the case for workers with a lack of job control.

the role of the psychosocial work environment in maintaining work ability and work performance among workers with decreased work abilities.
the role of job control in the relationship between decreased work ability due to disease and productivity loss at work.
the importance of job control to remain productive at the workplace despite a decrease in work ability.

the negative effects on work ability of chronic disease may be partly counteracted by increased job control.
workers with a decreased work ability are more likely to experience productivity loss at work when they have a lack of job control.

workers who experience decreased work ability can remain productive at work if they have a job with high control.
